consensus_summary: Anointing centrally signifies consecration or divine appointment to sacred office or service, normally joined with empowerment by the Holy Spirit; literal oil serves as its visible sign.
book_summary: Anointing marks a person or thing as belonging to God and appoints it to a specified office or work, while distinguishing the appointment itself from its visible sign, empowering Spirit, and resulting task.
consensus_core_identification: Divine consecration or appointment, characteristically accompanied by Spirit-given empowerment.
book_core_identification: Divine ownership and appointment to an office or work; oil and Spirit are respectively possible sign and power rather than the appointment itself.
boundary_disagreement: The book includes anointed objects and appointed agents even when no personal reception of the Spirit is stated, and it does not make Spirit-empowerment necessary to the definition. It also reclassifies oil, Spirit-power, office, and work as distinguishable aspects rather than folding them all into “the anointing.”
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction over the central category of consecration or appointment. The material difference is conditional: the consensus commonly joins anointing with Spirit-empowerment, whereas the book treats empowerment as possible but not constitutive.
rationale: Both readings identify anointing primarily with being set apart or appointed by God, so the central referent is preserved. The book nevertheless sharpens and broadens that category by making appointment the defining element and by separating it from oil as sign and the Spirit as power. This admits cases such as the tabernacle and Cyrus without requiring Spirit-empowerment in the same sense as David or Jesus, creating a real boundary refinement rather than a replacement of the consensus view.
strongest_objection: The consensus responses already mention sacred objects, literal ritual oil, and consecration independently of empowerment, so the book’s distinctions could be viewed as merely explicit wording of an existing consensus and therefore a MATCH. However, the book’s deliberate use of “may” and its warning against conflating appointment, sign, power, and office make the definitional boundary materially more precise.
